decisions.reasoning: ARIA's initial recon pass is SUPERFICIAL. Critical gaps: (1) Subdomain enumeration is INCOMPLETE — crt.sh returned 502 and ARIA stopped instead of using subfinder, amass, DNS brute-forcing, or alternative CT sources. No subdomains means no takeover validation and no expanded attack surface. (2) Tech stack reported as 'nginx' without a version — versionless fingerprinting blocks CVE matching downstream. (3) Cloud asset discovery (S3, Azure, GCP, Firebase) was not attempted. (4) JS file analysis for endpoints/API keys/hidden routes was not done. (5) Zone transfer (AXFR) on systemdns.com nameservers was recommended but not executed. (6) No breach database or credential search for exposed email ahmed.chiboub@cyberian-defenses.com. (7) No historical DNS lookup. The direct server exposure finding and security header analysis are thorough, and the email infrastructure analysis is adequate. But the missing items are foundational — without subdomains and versioned tech stack, Lisa and Bloodhound will be working with an incomplete map. Re-dispatch ARIA with explicit instructions to fill these gaps before routing to Lisa.

decisions.reasoning: ARIA has completed 2 recon cycles. Cycle 1 was superficial (crt.sh failed, no fallbacks). Cycle 2 produced better infrastructure mapping (confirmed direct server at 76.13.46.223, no WAF/CDN, Zoho email, DNS provider systemdns.com, security headers) but core gaps remain: no subdomains discovered, nginx version unknown, no cloud asset check, no JS analysis. However, ARIA reports that key tools (subfinder, amass, CertSpotter) are unavailable, meaning a third re-dispatch risks spinning wheels with the same tool limitations. Critically, Lisa's active scanning CAN fill the two most important gaps: (1) nginx version via service version detection / banner grab, (2) JS files and hidden endpoints via HTTP crawling and directory brute-forcing. Lisa can also discover subdomains via virtual host enumeration and DNS brute-forcing with gobuster/ffuf. The passive-only gaps (cloud asset discovery, breach/credential search, historical DNS) are secondary — they expand the attack surface but are not blockers for scanning the known target. Per decision criteria: 'If ARIA found no new targets and we've scanned common OSINT sources → scan.' We've exhausted available OSINT sources. ARIA's scope objections about AXFR against systemdns.com nameservers are overly cautious — querying authoritative nameservers about an in-scope domain is passive recon. But this is moot since AXFR is unlikely to succeed. Scope candidates: reject api.github.com (GitHub infrastructure, out of scope), reject 223.46.13.76 (unrelated IP, no association to target found), note cyberian-defenses.firebaseapp.com for investigation if Lisa finds Firebase references. Aggressiveness is cautious but target has no WAF/CDN so standard scanning is appropriate.

decisions.reasoning: Lisa completed scanning of cyberian-defenses.com (76.13.46.223). Findings: 3 TCP ports open (22/SSH 9.6p1, 80/HTTP nginx 1.24.0, 443/HTTPS nginx 1.24.0), all UDP closed. Strong TLS (A-grade, TLS 1.2+), CSP unsafe-inline, missing X-Frame-Options on port 80, developer email exposed (ahmed.chiboub@cyberian-defenses.com), /blog/ path found. Critical depth gaps: (1) gobuster failed — no directory enumeration was performed, (2) no vhost enumeration, (3) no JS file analysis, (4) /blog/ not investigated for CMS, (5) SSH algorithms/ciphers not checked, (6) cloud assets (S3/Azure/GCP buckets) not verified for access. These gaps map directly to Bloodhound and Wasp capabilities. Bloodhound can run nuclei, searchsploit, ssh-audit, and verify cloud bucket access. Wasp can run ffuf for directory brute-force, crawl JS files, test /blog/ for CMS vulns, and perform OWASP Top 10 testing. Routing to parallel vuln detection rather than re-dispatching Lisa — the vuln bots have better tool coverage for these web-layer gaps and can address them during their normal workflow. The target has a minimal attack surface but enough versioned services for meaningful CVE matching.
